utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Good morning. Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. Case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Miroslav Tadic, and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Can the witness make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Please sit down. Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir. Mr. Simic, can you please adjust your headphones. You'll hear better. Thank you very much. Will you please introduce yourself for the record.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: My name is Cedomir Simic, from Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You are Dr. Blagoje Simic's brother, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, today we shall be talking about the statement 92 bis, as per the instructions of the Trial Chamber, certain paragraphs and certain topics have to be discussed during your testimony before this Trial Chamber. Since we're speaking the same language, for the benefit of the interpreters, can you please make a short break after my question. In that way, we shall have an accurate record of your statement. Mr. Simic, you have given your detailed statement. You have signed it in the presence of the representatives of the Tribunal. However, for this case and for providing better information for this Trial Chamber, could you please answer the following questions that I'm going to put to you. In 1992, you were a member of a political party. What party was that?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: I was a member of the socialist party. That was the SDP. The president of that party was Nijaz Durakovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That was at the level of Bosnian Herzegovina, and those were the successors of the League of Communists; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Later on, in 1996, did you join another party?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Since this first party was frozen during 1992, I was not a member of any party up to 1996 or early 1997, and then I joined the Serbian Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: After that period, after 1997, generally speaking, did you join any other party? If so, what party was that?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: In 1998, I joined the ranks of Biljana Plavsic's party, i.e., the party of the Serbian democratic alliance. A fraction of that party became the democratic peoples alliance, and that is the party that I am a member of to this very day.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: For a number of years, you were the CEO of the trading company called Samcanka, and you held that same position in mid-April 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: I was the CEO from 1988, and the name of the company was Bosanka, the Bosanka company. During 1992, the Bosanka company became the Samcanka trading company. I continued serving as the CEO of that company.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Currently you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, do not repeat what is in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Because you are only taking up your time, and you have one hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, for your instructions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: This witness would have been very brief if you stuck to what was required to testify on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'll take care about that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Currently you are a member of the municipal administration of Samac municipality?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. I am the chief of the department for economy of the municipality of Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simic, were you a member of the 4th Detachment in 1992?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: When were you mobilised?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly, but I received my call-up papers sometime in March 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me: Where were you on the night between the 16th and the 17th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: During that night, I was at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In the morning, in the early morning hours of that night, on the 17th of April, around 3.00 in the morning, there was an armed conflict in Samac, and that is not disputable. What did you do at that moment? Did you do anything?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: As I said, I was at home that night, and it was only in the morning, since the telephones didn't work, did I find out from the courier that the forces of the 17th Tactical Group occupied certain points in the town of Samac. That was a preventive measure on their part.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: When you say the 17th Tactical Group, who do you mean? How many detachments were there in that Tactical Group, if you know?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: I don't know how many troops were there, how many detachments were there, but I know that this was a regular army and that there were also volunteers from Serbia there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: When the courier from the 4th Detachment came, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: I was told to stay at home. And since my area is densely populated, other neighbours, other members of the detachment, were also told to stay at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me: What happened next, over the next few days? Did somebody come to fetch you? Were you told what you were supposed to do? Can you tell us briefly what happened?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: On the 18th of April, 1992, a police vehicle came with one policeman in it. He came to fetch me, and the explanation was that I was needed by the president of the Executive Board, Mr. Mirko Jovanovic, and that I was to report to the agricultural combine. Together with this policeman, I went to the agricultural combine and I found a large group of deputies and businessmen there. And after a short conversation, the then president of the Executive Board, Mirko Jovanovic, invited a number of business people to follow him to the Municipal Assembly building. There we discussed the ways to provide for the normalisation of life in the area of the municipality as far as the institutions and the companies were concerned, and the supply of the population with staple foods. This was also discussed in the Municipal Assembly building.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: If you remember, can you please tell us: During that meeting with the president of the Executive Board, Mr. Mirko Jovanovic, who else was there? Who were the other business people, CEOs of various companies who were there at that time?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: I remember that in the office of the president of the Executive Board, there was Milan Simic, Mirko Lukic. There were directors Juro Krajinovic, the director of Velopromet; then Pero Vasiljevic, the CEO of the department store; and I believe there was Stefan Tutnjevic from the agricultural combine.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could you please slow down for the record. Let's just correct some things in the record. Tell me. Juro Krajinovic was the CEO of what company?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Velopromet. Of the three trading companies, Velopromet was a wholesale company which supplied the other two trading companies with goods.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Juro Krajinovic is of what ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: He is a Croat and he had been the director of that company for two or three years before the beginning of war operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And another correction in the transcript, please. What was the name of the director of the department store? Can you please pronounce his name slowly for the record.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: The director of the department store was Pero Vasiljevic [Realtime transcript read in error missing word "Vasiljevic"].

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Although we have had a lot of testimonies speaking about the atmosphere in Samac during those days, could you please tell us something about the situation in your company that prevailed at that time. As far as I understood, your company -- I apologise. My colleague has drawn my attention to the fact that in your answer --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It's just for the record. It's page 6, line 11. After the name Pero, it should be his family name Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I wonder, Mr. Simic, could you tell us what the name of the agricultural combine was that you were asked to go to the meeting at.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The agricultural combine was the industrial and agricultural combine of Bosanski Samac. That was its name then and that is still its name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So follow up on this question of the Honourable Judge Williams, in the popular jargon, wasn't the abbreviation for that company PIK?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was the industrial and agricultural combine.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: But in the every day conversations, people do not use the long name. They call this company PIK, don't they, P-I-K?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: We've heard a lot of testimonies talking about the situation during those days in Samac, fighting started, and we will not go over that ground, because that is not the topic of your testimony. However, your company was very specific. You had a number of retail shops in town. How did the situation reflect on the activities of your company? What did you do in order to bring the situation in your company to some sort of a normal situation?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: On the 18th and 19th of April, 1992, I had some conversation with the president of the Executive Board, and we agreed that we should try our utmost to provide the population with staple foods in order to provide for the normal life in town. So all of our retail shops had to be open and accessible to the population. They had to serve their needs. We also agreed that certain measures should be taken in respect of the state companies and institutions which operated in Samac, this with a view to provide for the normal operation of these companies. The Hranaprodukt company was given the most attention. This company is the processing company for the processing of food and vegetables. And during power cuts, all of their stocks were -- could perish. Also we agreed to take certain measures in the industrial and agricultural combine, because there was a certain number of head of cattle for which we had to provide water and fodder. There were over 400 bulls which had to be fed. We also talked about the Uniglas company, the factory for the processing of glass panels for cars. The shelling had already started, and we saw that the complete stock of that company came under threat. Therefore, we had to take measures for these glass panels to be secured.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Very well, then, Mr. Simic. Mr. Simic, you're an experienced businessman. Let us try to draw a conclusion. A number of CEOs and members of the Executive Boards took all the measures they could to prevent possible damage from occurring and to save the property of all those companies?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Next question, vital to our case, is the following: How many retail shops were there within the framework of your company, in the Samac territory?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Prior to the outbreak of war operations --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. I must interrupt you here. I'm talking about the period after the war had broken out. How many of your retail shops were still in operation? That's what I want to know.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: In the territory of Samac municipality, after the outbreak of war operations, I don't know the exact number, but about 45 retail shops in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Immediately after the 17th of April, those retail shops, can you please tell the Trial Chamber: What was the predominant nationality of the employees in those retail shops, both the managers and the common employees?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: The entire company of Bosanka, and this includes the retail shops, all three ethnic groups were represented: Serbs, Croats, and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me: What was the role of putting -- of keeping the companies as efficient as possible, with a view to supplying the civilian population of Samac municipality with staple goods? What was the situation? What were the needs of the civilian population and how did that function on a day-to-day basis?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: After the outbreak of war operations, and after we talked to the president of the Executive Board, we took all the measures available to us to keep the shops open and to provide the citizens with staple goods. There was a commission, an appointed commission, which went door to door, activating workers and managers who were materially responsible for the goods, for keeping the shops open, for providing citizens with the necessary goods.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Were citizens of all three ethnic backgrounds in the same position in as far as their access to those shops? Were all three ethnic backgrounds or nationalities allowed to use your shops, the shops owned by your company?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: I state this with full responsibility. As far as our retail shops were concerned, our workers, our managers, no distinction was ever made with respect to people's ethnic backgrounds. At that time, we really cared about keeping our shops open and providing citizens with goods, throughout the municipal territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In your company, who was the chief of finances?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: The chief of the financial sector in my company, throughout the war and even now, is Jusufovic [as interpreted], B.A. in economics. He is a Muslim by nationality.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Just for the record, Your Honour, it's page 10, line 4. The complete name of the person mentioned by this witness is Jusuf Jusufovic. Jusuf is the name and Jusufovic is the family name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please tell me: In your company, you mentioned that there were all the different nationalities, but Mr. Sego was also one of the managers. Can you please tell us which official position he held?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Drago Sego, throughout the whole period under observation here, was our cashier in the Bosanka company. Since 1988. Today he is a retired employee of the same company.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: During 1992 and 1993, these closest colleagues of yours, closest collaborators who had a lot of authority, one of them was a Croat and one of them was a Muslim, kept working for your company without any difficulty at all?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell the Trial Chamber: In 1991, 1992, and 1993, the employees of your company, were they paid salaries in return for their work?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: All those employed by our company had work obligations or assignments. I was the head of that company and the same applied to me and to all the other employees. We had our book of rules concerning awards given to employees. All employees were paid their regular salary, their meals, and we provided all the other incentives that we could throughout that period to our employees. No distinction was made on the basis of someone's nationality.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Throughout that period, were the contributions for the pension fund and for the social insurance also paid to your workers?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Pursuant to the laws, all the contributions were being paid, the supplements for the health insurance and for the pension fund of those employees.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You talked about the war assignment or the war obligation -- the work assignment or the work obligation. Did you also have a work obligation as the head of that company?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: The decision on the work assignment, did that go through the office [as interpreted] of the Ministry of Defence in Samac, the local office?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Just for the record, instead of word "office" in page 11, line 18, should be "detachment" of -- municipal detachment of Ministry of Defence. Just for the clarification. Otherwise everything is okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So all the employees, all the remaining employees, had received decisions from the Ministry of Defence for their work, the continuation of their activities?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You personally, throughout 1992 and 1993 - and that's what we're looking at now for the needs of this case - did you only have a work obligation or did your daily activity cover something else too?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have a problem because the channel we're using to listen to the B/C/S translation, we are now receiving French translation. I'm not sure about the witness, but we here do have a technical problem and we're listening to the French translation on channel 6. So if you could please check this with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I'll repeat my question, and you, Mr. Simic, please tell me if there is a problem in terms of the translation you're receiving.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Everything is perfectly fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Very well. I'll go back to my previous question. In 1992 and 1993, aside from having been assigned your work obligation as the head of the company, what were your other duties?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: I had a military obligation too. I had a military obligation as a soldier, and my assignment was to go to the line of defence, around Grebnice.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: As far as I understand, that was the front line.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: This strikes me as slightly strange, if I may say, but I have to explain this to the Trial Chamber. You were the manager, the head of this very important company. You had a work obligation, but at the same time you had received a war assignment, and you had to risk your life on the front line. Please, can you explain this?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'd object, Your Honour. Who is testifying here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic. The question -- the objection is that the question was leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, can you please tell the Trial Chamber: How did this come about, you having both a work obligation and a war, or rather, military assignment? Briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: No exceptions were made. All those who were of military age and able-bodied had to go to the line of defence, and those who could keep working in the companies kept on working. I had a work obligation in my company, but I also had a war assignment, a military assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please: What do you know about the fact that with the hyperinflation galloping in 1992 and 1993, how were salaries paid to people? How did that happen under those difficult circumstances in 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: With hyperinflation, with war economy, while the existing infrastructure was being destroyed and, on the other hand, with the growing needs of the population throughout the period for staple foods, for communal services, for medicines - we're talking about the health centre and the hospital - pursuant to a request of the Executive Board, a solution had to be found how to provide and supply the goods with galloping hyperinflation by the hour, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: We'll come to that later, but now I want to know about the following: In view of the hyperinflation and the devaluation of salaries, how did you compensate the workers for their salaries? Can you tell us about that? What sort of remuneration did they get?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, in view of their salary, the employees were given the equivalent value in goods, goods that were necessary to live on in those circumstances, and the same applied to myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Another topic which is relevant for this case, at least the Defence believe so, the concept of state-owned companies, or state-run companies. In 1992 and 1993, what was the structure of the large companies that you have spoken about and other companies in the Samac area? I'm talking about the companies of considerable size.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: The whole of the local economy, before the war, was based on state-owned companies. Actually, socially owned enterprises and later they became state-owned companies. So I repeat: All the local economy in the Samac area was based on the socially owned enterprises.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What was the role of Samac municipality in terms of appointing managers and CEOs to these socially owned enterprises? Was there any kind of relationship at work there?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Based on the war laws and on instructions by the relevant ministries, the Executive Board appointed coordinators to these companies, so that all the socially owned enterprises and companies had their own coordinator or war manager.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: The next question following up, a follow-up question: Did the Executive Board also appoint coordinators to privately owned companies, or did this only apply to the socially owned enterprises and companies?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: This only applied to the socially owned ones, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me briefly, please: The Ministry of Defence of Republika Srpska, did they have provisions regulating the functioning of the economy in terms of the needs of the Ministry of Defence in wartime? Can you tell us anything about that?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, we had very strict war laws, wartime laws and regulations, which applied to the economy, to production, to the placement of goods, and to securing the needs of the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell us about the activities of your own company pursuant to requests of the military administration in Odzak. Were there any obligations you had to meet there?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Based on the information that we had in the area of Odzak municipality, people were returning there, and the Executive Board made a request for us to open three shops, to open up three shops in the area, general goods, to meet the needs of the population returning there and supplying goods for the population only in the area of Odzak municipality in that particular period.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Please tell us: On the territory of the municipality of Samac - and I'm speaking about the area which belonged to the Serb part - was there a production? What was being produced in various companies and firms, according to you?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: After the normalisation of life in wartime, with regards to the supplying of hospitals, with medicine and food staples for various companies, we had to accomplish springtime sowing, and this usually happens in April and in May. So we had to make sure that the sowing was not postponed, because in that time, it means that when we talk about various foods, we would not be able to produce it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Is there a company which produces boilers in Samac?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: No. Let us get to the point. Is there a company which produces boilers?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. The company is called Mebos and it produces boilers in Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: During the year of 1992 and 1993, was the production of boilers made -- repeated in that company?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Were these products being sold?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Who was the intermediary? Who was making sure that the products of that company were placed on the marketplace?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, the exchanges were necessary at the time, and the Executive Board created a company in Stara Pazova, and Radul Smiljkovic became the CEO of that company. He was from Serbia. That company was the intermediary with regards to the placement of boilers on the marketplace and other products.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Stara Pazova is in Serbia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Please tell me: When products stemming from the municipality of Samac, and when they were placed on the marketplace through that intermediary, what did you need for the needs of the population? For instance, if you sell boilers, what do you get in exchange?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: When we were selling boilers in that particular case, the priority was given to staple foods and consumer goods, as well as the medication for pharmaceutical purposes, and other material needed for the production of boilers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Aside from the production of boilers, in 1992, in 1993, in Samac, was there any other type of production made?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. The industry of furniture existed, and still exists today. Buducnost is a company which produced upholstered furniture and various different types of furniture, and that company was opened during the war, and it is still open today.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Since Samac was in an area which was predominantly an agricultural area, can you tell us if those products were also being sold and exchanged on the marketplace?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: I would like to say that the fattened bulls were particularly interesting, and they came from the combine of Samac. And Hranaprodukt, there was a deep-freeze programme for various foods, and that was the exchange that existed in Stara Pazova.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us: What kind of pharmaceutical products were made, or what is that the hospitals needed and what did that company provide to supply various hospitals for the needs of your area and of foreign countries?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Our area is a risky area for a disease with -- in terms of --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I have to interrupt you because I will have to repeat my question. I'm not satisfied with the translation of my question. Please tell the court: What kind of medical supplies did that company produce in Stara Pazova for the needs of Serbia, the area of Serbia, and also for the needs of foreign countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I'll repeat my question in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could you tell the Chamber, please, for the hospital needs, which kind of products, medical products, this company from Stara Pazova that you mentioned import from Serbia and from foreign countries? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: We have a dialysis centre in Samac. We had made a particular attention for the providing of haemodialysis for the life support of people who needed dialysis. We were able to get various products in medication from haemofarm Vrsac and they were producing dialysis material. And we were able to get also various pharmaceutical products which we were able to distribute to the medical centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since the Executive Board gave you certain instructions with regards to the war economy, could you please tell us if Blagoje Simic was able to influence in a certain way the work of the executive committee? Was he able, for instance, to give certain orders or to make a difference in terms of the decisions that would be brought by the Executive Board?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: It was practically impossible that Dr. Blagoje Simic takes part in the distribution of the needs of the municipality in terms of staple foods to the distribution of the municipality, with regards to the medication and other material. According to the laws of war, the Executive Board was an institution --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'd object at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: He's going to start discussing the laws of war? There is no -- there's no indication of any background that he has as a lawyer, that he's received any legal training. It's outside the scope of his testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: No, no, no, Your Honour. It is not discussion of the laws of war. It is simply a personal knowledge of a well-experienced manager and a member of some Executive Board institutions, with his personal knowledge what was the relation between the relevant ministries on the governmental level and local level with Executive Board. His personal knowledge as a well-experienced manager on that field. Nothing -- we are not speaking about laws of war, we are not speaking about legal issues. We are just speaking about his personal knowledge of what and how this relation was actually -- and we hear that from many witnesses here, from the same area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no objection if he's going to speak from his experience. You know, he can say based on my experience in Samac, this usually happened. However, he stated, on line 19, 1, "according to the laws of war." If he's going to give a legal opinion, we would object.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. That's a matter of translation. I do apologise to my learned friend. I never said -- and that's a nonsense, absolute nonsense. Why should I use --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No. The witness said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That's a problem of translation. He said that in fact it was economical regulation during the state of war. That's the proper translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: We shall clarify that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So he will stick to his experience; he will stick to the facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are talking about laws, regulations, which were linked to the economy, which prevailed during the war, and I asked you if Dr. Blagoje Simic was able to have any type of influence on the work of the Executive Board and on the coordination, given his role as president of the Crisis Staff. And please tell us from your own experience, what do you know during 1992 and 1993? Would you please briefly explain this to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: According to my own knowledge, the Executive Board was the organ which was able to have -- they had at its disposal all the material needs, and they were able to distribute that to the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How often did you used to see your brother during those wartime years in 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Blagoje and myself, we are brothers. I am his older brother. I'm 11 years older than him. I have my own profession. I'm an agronomist. He has his own profession. And we would see each other during family meetings. More rarely in Samac, but more frequently in Kruskovo Polje, which was our family house.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: As a brother, did Dr. Blagoje Simic ever complain to you about some problems? Because, of course, you remember living in difficult times. As brothers, would you exchange your points of view? Was he complaining about something to you?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, we had our family discussions whenever we would meet, and we would always meet with the rest of our family.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Please tell us: Do you know if Dr. Blagoje Simic, as a president of the Crisis Staff, did he order the arrest of some people or the mistreatment of certain individuals on the territory of Samac, the municipality of Samac?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: I can confirm to you that my brother, Blagoje Simic, never ordered that somebody gets killed. He never killed anyone. And he never carried out any type of discrimination on the municipality of Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And please tell us if during those first days after the outbreak of the conflict, in the month of April of 1992, did you get a phone call from the brother of Sulejman Tihic? And if he did call you, tell us why did he call you. What did he want from you, and what transpired from that conversation?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: After the outbreak of the conflict, war conflict, Bato, the brother of Sulejman Tihic, called me. I don't know his name. That's only his nickname. And he asked me something about Blagoje Simic. I said that I didn't know where Blagoje was, and that was really the fact. I didn't know where Blagoje was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did you suggest something to the brother of Sulejman Tihic at that time?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: He then asked me if Sulejman Tihic could come to my house, because we were neighbours. I told him that I have nothing against that, but the front line from the village of Prud was nearby, and the army would often come there. He then changed his mind, and Sulejman and himself changed their minds, so they did not come to my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I've finished my examination-in-chief for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Before you actually sit down, I just have one point of clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: On page 20, your question, Mr. Pantelic, beginning on line 11 through to line 17, I don't believe you got an answer to it. You had a couple of questions all linked together, and I don't believe you got an answer to the question, which is as follows: You were asking Mr. Simic if Dr. Blagoje Simic was able to have any type of influence on the work of the Executive Board and the coordination, given his role as president of the Crisis Staff? As far as I'm concerned, the answer did not address that. Mr. Simic only addressed the second question that you posed. So perhaps if Mr. Simic could answer that question, it would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. I'm very grateful for your intervention, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, so the question was to the effect whether Dr. Blagoje Simic had any type of influence through his position, and was he able to coordinate the work of the Executive Board?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, the Executive Board worked according to the order that was given from the government at the time, and it was an independent institution. It had at its disposal needs, supplies. And when it comes to the economy, Blagoje Simic could not have had any direct nor any indirect influence on the economy of the municipality of Samac.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I do apologise. Just a last question with regard to this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you know if at the time the Executive Board was reporting to the Crisis Staff, was it informing them what was going on with regards to the humanitarian aspect, social aspects, and the economy?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: As the coordinator, the president of the Executive Board was calling us for meetings, and he would give us concrete tasks. So I do not know if -- or rather, I don't know what was the link between the Executive Board and the Crisis Staff, what was the relationship between the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I've finished with examination-in-chief of this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I was going to wait and see if Defence counsel were going to question. Mr. Lukic stood up.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I merely wanted to inform the Trial Chamber that we, for our part, have no questions for Mr. Simic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Simic. I will ask you a few brief questions, referring mostly to your membership in the 4th Detachment, or rather, the events on the 17th of April, 1992. You said yourself that your house is in a densely populated area of the town of Bosanski Samac. This district, this neighbourhood where your house is, is it generally known as Sljivik?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that among your neighbours, regardless of their ethnic background, there was a number of members of the 4th Detachment of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you know whether any of those members of the 4th Detachment in any way whatsoever, on the 17th of April, took part in any kind of military operation in the town of Samac, or did you see all of them in the morning when you were there?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: On the 17th of April, 1992, in the morning, about 5.00, a messenger came and told us not to leave our homes for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: He told you, as in you or the others too?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: He conveyed instructions and orders to me, because I was at home, and I assume also to other neighbours, those, at least, who were members of the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Those neighbours of yours, were they at home too?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you know, because your house was near the front line, the line of defence of the town of Samac, near the embankment, the members of the 4th Detachment, in the afternoon, did they deploy along the line of defence, along the embankment on the Bosna River, the right bank?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: There was a certain amount of commotion there. Some of them left of their own volition for the embankment, because it was only 10 or 15 metres away from their homes. I didn't leave home before I received orders telling me to do otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, you did not leave your home on the 17th until, on the 18th, a police vehicle came to pick you up and it took you to the PIK.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You have testified that you heard from the messenger that military forces of the 17th Tactical Group had taken vital buildings and facilities in the town of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: The witness said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think the witness just confirmed this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: If I heard you correctly, you said that on the 17th, in the morning, a messenger or courier came and told you that forces of the 17th Tactical Group had taken a number of facilities or buildings in the town of Samac as some kind of pre-emptive action, together with the volunteers. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you actually hear this afterwards, the same thing, from the commander of the 4th Detachment, from the deputy of the 4th Detachment or from the commander of the 17th Tactical Group?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: I had no occasion to hear this from any of the persons you have just enumerated.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Simic. My name is Phillip Weiner. I'm with the Office of the Prosecutor. I'm going to be asking you some questions for the next hour. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in your statement and in your testimony this morning, sir, you didn't indicate that you had been involved in politics as early as 1990. In 1990, you were a candidate for the Municipal Assembly; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: May the witness please be shown Exhibit P8 ter. The section in the back with all the candidates for the political office, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, you testified that after the Communist Party, you joined the Socialist Party. Would you please look at that list from the Official Gazette, and you'll notice under number 16, it says "Cedomir Simic, Serb, Bosanski Samac." Is that you?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I do apologise. I don't have any objection for this line of questioning, but for the sake of clarity, we would like to have a B/C/S version of this Official Gazette, because otherwise it's nothing. I mean, it's just a list. I don't know from where it comes. Maybe I can check Official Gazette. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Actually, you could use mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: This is -- I thought this is a page -- part of Exhibit P8, or what is it, Mr. Weiner?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I thought this was one of the pages of Exhibit P8.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, it's one of the pages of Exhibit P8. It's just a list of names.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could I have a copy of my learned friend in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Why don't you take mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, you don't have Exhibit P8? Because it's one of the documents already admitted into evidence and you're supposed to have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I cannot locate the exact page in B/C/S language, so that's a problem. Thank you. But thanks to my learned friend, we have our B/C/S version. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner. You can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, is that your name, Cedomir Simic, Serb, Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So you were a candidate in 1990 for the Municipal Assembly, under the Socialist Party?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And at that same time, your brother, the defendant Blagoje Simic, ran on the SDS ticket; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And he ran -- actually, his name was the first candidate listed on the SDS ticket. He was given that honour, the first candidate listed; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And he was elected, and as you know, he later became a member of the Crisis Staff, in fact its president.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you also know that your cousin Simeon Simic was a candidate in that election in 1990; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let me refresh your recollection. One moment, please. I ask you to look at the list of candidates, also in Exhibit P8, under the SSO party, and you'll see the first name on that ballot, and the SSO party is Simeon Simic and he's also listed like you and your brother as a Serb from Bosanski Samac. Isn't that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: I'm looking at this document now, but there's a lot that I still haven't seen, so I can't say that I'm particularly updated.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But do you see his name there as the number one candidate in the SSO party, Simeon Simic, a Serb from Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you're also aware, sir, that he was elected to the Assembly? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, do you recall that he later became a member of the Crisis Staff and served with your brother, the defendant Blagoje Simic?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: I saw him on the premises of the Municipal Assembly, but as to what he was doing there, I actually don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, after the Municipal Assembly was established in 1991, were you aware that in 1992 he became a member of the Crisis Staff and served with your brother, the defendant Blagoje Simic?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: I repeat: I did see him in the Municipal Assembly building, but I do not know what he was doing there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And when you say you saw him, do you mean 1992, in the spring or early summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: The beginning of summer 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, your cousin Milan Simic was not a candidate in 1990, but you are aware that he became the president of the Executive Board?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: I'm aware of that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And he also attended Crisis Staff meetings with your cousin Simeon and your brother Blagoje; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And your brother, the defendant Simic, has testified that Milan Simic, your cousin, was related to Stevan Todorovic, the police chief? Are you aware of that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. We have a clear ruling with regard to the previous witness statement, including the defendant, with regard to the questioning of the witness. So maybe we could follow that rule. I mean, if my learned friend has some idea or line of questioning, he can be very directly, what is the personal knowledge of this witness with regard to such-and-such meetings and this or that occasion. Otherwise it's not in accordance with the practice, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'm not confronting him. I'm just asking him about his family tree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic. That's what I was -- I was looking at the formation of the question itself. It wasn't a form of impeachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I agree with you absolutely. But on -- it's page 30, line 1, just the word "has testified" that Milan Simic, et cetera, et cetera. So maybe we could be focused just on the event or the particular isolated fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, to keep things moving, I'll just rephrase the question so we can just move along.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, Stevan Todorovic married Milan Simic's family, into the Simic family; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: They were not in-laws? Your brother indicated that they were in-laws. Do you recall any sort of wedding?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: It's the other way around. Milan Simic married into Stevan Todorovic's family, because he is his brother-in-law. Stevan Todorovic is single, so he could not have married into anyone's family. So it's the other way around, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So Milan Simic married -- based on Milan Simic's marriage, he and Stevan Todorovic are now related; correct? Okay. And are you aware that Stevan Todorovic, who is now related to the Simic family, also was attending Crisis Staff meetings?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: I did see Stevan Todorovic likewise in the town of Samac and on the premises of the Municipal Assembly, but I do not know why he was there, and I do not know that he attended any meetings of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, do you know a man from Batkusa named Aco Jankovic? Aco?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Aco Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And he was also a relative of Milan Simic, your cousin Milan Simic?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: I do know Aco Jankovic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you also know that he was a cousin or a relative of Milan Simic too, some sort of relative?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, I know that he is some kind of relative of Milan Simic's wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And were you aware that Aco Jankovic was also present at one or more Crisis Staff meetings and was assisting the Crisis Staff in some manner?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, we've discussed your brother; yourself; your cousins Simeon, Milan, Stevan Todorovic, Aco Jankovic. Were there any other members of your family involved in municipal government in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So just those?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. I mean, it's not fair to this witness. I can find how this witness is related to Aco Jankovic or Stevan Todorovic. And by the way, just to help my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The witness has already explained, so -- the witness has already explained, so there is no basis for your objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let's move on, sir. You testified that you were not a member of the SDS party; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: I was not a member of the SDS until 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And back in 1991, 1992, you didn't attend any SDS meetings; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you never attended any SDS board meetings back at that same time, municipal board meetings?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you were never present with your brother, the defendant Blagoje Simic, when he met or spoke with any SDS leaders, were you?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you were never with your brother, you were never present with your brother, when he met with other SDS members and they had certain types of meetings or planning or strategy sessions?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, were you aware that the SDS party was involved in the establishment of the Serbian municipality of Samac?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. My employees told me about it, my employees who were working in the field, but I did not hear about this from Blagoje Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you also knew, sir, that the SDS party was involved in the establishment of the Crisis Staff in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were you aware that your brother, as SDS president, was involved in the establishment of the Crisis Staff for the Serbian municipality of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And were you aware that your brother was elected Municipal Assembly president on April 14th, at the initiative of the SDS party municipal board?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you've testified today, and in your 92 bis statement you've described the powers of the executive committee, or you used the phrase executive committee, but we've been using Executive Board here. And in fact, in paragraph 16 to 21, you describe the powers of the executive committee.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: If the witness would like to see his statement, it's 163/1 ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, could you look at that, and in paragraph 16 to 21, we've redacted, which is they have removed paragraph 20 from your statement and they have taken your testimony instead of paragraph 20. So paragraphs basically 16 to 21 you describe the powers of the Executive Board, the powers and functions of the Executive Board. Correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you also mention the Executive Board in paragraphs 1, 10, and 15.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Approximately 40 per cent of the paragraphs contained in your statement you mention the Executive Board. That's 8 of approximately 21, 37 per cent, 40 per cent. You mention the Executive Board. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: I have not tried to calculate the exact percentage, but I suppose you must be right on that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, sir, nowhere in that statement do you mention that your brother, the defendant Blagoje Simic, served as the president of the Crisis Staff and the War Presidency. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And sir, even though you mention the Executive Board in approximately 37 per cent of the paragraphs in that report, in that written statement, you don't mention the Crisis Staff or the War Presidency, the two boards that your brother served as president, even once, you don't mention the War Presidency or the Crisis Staff. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: The nature of my work or my tasks during wartime was to receive my tasks from the Executive Board, and that's why I tried to clarify as most as I could this particular segment of the work and tasks assigned by the Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: However, sir, you never mention the Crisis Staff or the War Presidency even once in that written statement. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: I suppose it's true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, I'm wondering about this line of questioning of the witness, because I was under the impression that he had instructions on what matters to discuss in his Rule 92 bis statement, and also in complying with the provisions of the Rule, to avoid the activities and conduct of the accused, since he was -- he could have been acting as president of those two institutions. Perhaps that's the reason why the witness avoided discussing that at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I was going to ask him that next. However, Your Honour, since he did discuss that and then there are other matters that we're going to contest very soon, it's now time for a break, you'll see why this is very relevant. We are going to contest some of the things he said, indicating he's either lied or he's been mistaken in his statement or his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps -- yes. The cross-examination can go along those lines, but I just wanted to explain perhaps to be fair to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I think it's time for the break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We shall take our break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Good morning. Let's continue on. We were talking about the Crisis Staff, the War Presidency, and the Executive Board. Now, sir, were you aware that the highest organ of authority in the Serbian municipality of Samac was the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you knew that the Crisis Staff had replaced the Assembly, so it then became the highest organ of authority in the municipality. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And sir, you also knew that the War Presidency, when it replaced the Crisis Staff, it then became the highest organ of authority in the Serbian municipality of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And sir, were you aware that the Assembly in the Serbian municipality of Samac was required to decide on the organisation and work of the Executive Board? Were you aware of that? And that's according to the Official Gazette of August 1994, which describes that period. Were you aware of that, that the Assembly was required to decide on the organisation and work of the Executive Board?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, were you aware that the Crisis Staff, which replaced the Serbian municipality, was required to exercise political control over the work of the Executive Board, and that's also according to the Official Gazette, which is P125 in this case? Were you aware of that, that the Crisis Staff was required to exercise political control over the work of the Executive Board?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And when you talk about the powers of the Executive Board, were you aware that the Crisis Staff had the power to annul or cancel any Executive Board decision if it was not in conformity with the constitution, the regulations of the Republic or any Crisis Staff decisions, they had the power to cancel or annul? Were you aware of those powers of the Crisis Staff to annul or cancel decisions of the Executive Board?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, were you aware that the Crisis Staff appointed the president and vice-president of the Executive Board?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you knew that your cousin Milan Simic was appointed president of the Executive Board by the Crisis Staff; you knew that?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: I know he was appointed president of the Executive Board, but I don't know by whom.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So you weren't aware, sir, that the Crisis Staff appointed Milan Simic the president of the Executive Board? In fact, your brother, the defendant Blagoje Simic, signed that notice of appointment. You didn't know that?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: No, I did not analyse the procedure to appoint president of the Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So when you discuss the powers of the Executive Board, you never mention the powers of the Crisis Staff and War Presidency in relation to the Executive Board and how the Executive Board answered to the Crisis Staff and War Presidency. You never mentioned that in your 92 bis statement.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: I could not mention that in my statement because I was not familiar with all that. The only contacts I had were with the president of the Executive Board, when he invited coordinators to assign tasks to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So even though you mention the powers of the Executive Board, you were not aware or you didn't understand or realise that it was subordinated to the Crisis Staff or War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: What I understood was that the orders given to us by the president of the Executive Board were to be carried out by us, and also that the Executive Board acted in accordance with law and that it issued orders based on the instructions of the governmental institutions and ministries.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But you didn't know that it carried out the orders of the Crisis Staff and the War Presidency, or do you include that in the governmental institutions that it implements their instructions?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: The basic task of the Executive Board, according to my understanding, was to implement instructions of the ministries at the level of the republican government.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So you weren't aware of the local legislation or the local statutes and laws and rules in relation to the Executive Board and the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: I had too many obligations, so I did not concern myself with political decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So my question is, once again: You were not aware of the local legislation or local statutes and laws and rules in relation to the Executive Board and the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. Finally I must object, because according to the legislation at that time, there was not local laws. So my friend should be more specific with the questioning of this witness. That's point number one. Point number two: This witness is not a legal expert or constitutional expert, so maybe we could go on the other topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: There is no basis for your objection, Mr. Pantelic. The question as put by the Prosecution to the witness is perfectly all right. The less interruption we have, the better.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, yes or no: You were not familiar with those laws, regulations, statutes of the powers or the relationship between the Executive Board and the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'd like to refer you to paragraph 10 of your written statement, 163/1. And in paragraph 10, you claim that the Executive Board appointed you to serve as business coordinator?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask one copy for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sorry. I thought he had it. Sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, the registry informs the Trial Chamber that you haven't provided the statement of this witness with the paragraph struck out. You haven't provided that to the registry or to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In that case, Your Honour, I have to check with my case manager and during the break I will provide enough copies. So just for the record, only paragraph 20 was struck out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: In the meantime, we'll use the old statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And I won't refer to the redacted paragraph or the redacted version of the -- the stricken paragraph, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you were appointed -- you claim that the executive committee appointed you to serve as business coordinator of Bosanka retail. In fact, sir, you were appointed to your position by the Crisis Staff; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You were made the Crisis Staff coordinator of Bosanka retail; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: I became coordinator for the work of Bosanka, and I was appointed by the Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: It was your job to organise the work and business transactions of Bosanka, and those transactions had to be approved by the Crisis Staff of the municipality of Samac; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Isn't it a fact that your work -- in your work, you were responsible to the Crisis Staff? Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: No, it is not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: With the help of the usher, I'd like to show this document appointing him to his position by the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could we have the reference of this document? Is it exhibit? Is it a P exhibit or -- sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You've had it for weeks. It's a new document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: For weeks?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: When did you find this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I found it approximately three weeks ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: When was it disclosed to the --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Is he objecting to it or is he trying to --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's an objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, he's objecting because --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It's objecting on the same basis as a couple of days before, so I don't know what we are speaking here. Where is the obligation of the disclosure on the Prosecution, where is the receipt that it was disclosed years ago, from 1998 or maybe if my learned friend can say from which period of time he's in possession of that. It's a matter of principle. It's objection on the basis of principle, that we also raised two or three days ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner. We've had this problem before.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The document which was produced a few days ago was produced on the day the witness was going to testify. They have had this document at least two weeks. They've had the opportunity to show this document to the witness and to discuss this document with the witness. This document had not been given much earlier and it was not required to be given much earlier. This is not a Rule 68 or exculpatory evidence issue. It was not even relevant -- this document was not relevant until the 92 bis statement was analysed. Is there any infairness at this time? No. The defendant has had this statement for approximately two weeks. He's had the opportunity, as I said, to discuss it with the witness, to research the document. The document comes from the Crisis Staff of Bosanski Samac. He had the opportunity to show it to the witness, allow the witness to modify his statement, and he had the chance to have the witness indicate that the document was incorrect or question the authenticity of the document. This statement should not be suppressed, for three reasons: Without this document being admitted, Your Honour, false information, be it the result of a mistake or a lie, will be allowed into evidence. This document also raises questions as to the witness's credibility in relation to who hired him and the powers of the executive committee, which he discusses -- which he mentions and discusses in almost 40 per cent of the paragraphs in his 92 bis statement. Finally, the Defence is asking for what you could discuss as almost some sort of equitable relief. He is just talking about fairness. Well, let's talk about fairness. Let's talk about fairness starting today. In that 92 bis statement, there was no discussion of the 4th Detachment. However, there was discussion, there was testimony this morning about the 4th Detachment. In his 92 bis statement -- Your Honour, he's gone well beyond his 92 bis statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, I don't think that is necessary. Let's deal with this document. This document, as you say, merely deals with his appointment by the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Correct. It has no -- it wouldn't have been relevant but for his 92 bis statement. It is not an exculpatory document and he doesn't have reciprocal discovery, even though we've treated him, the Prosecution has treated the Defence of Blagoje Simic as if it has reciprocal discovery, he's not entitled to reciprocal discovery. So he's received the document two weeks. Once again, it wasn't relevant until his 92 bis statement was filed and analysed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, he doesn't have standing to object to this issue. It doesn't concern his client. I'd object to any comment from fellow defendants on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. Let's hear him. Maybe it has nothing to do with this document, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I must say that it does have to do with this document. First of all, I don't know what this document is all about, but what I heard from Mr. Weiner, it is about the Crisis Staff and this is very relevant for the defence of my client. That's why I wanted to say a few words. I'm really taken by surprise and I don't believe that this does not concern my client unless the Prosecution wants to exclude him from anything that has to do with the Crisis Staff. My previous objections, my defence is according to the Rule 66 on reciprocal disclosure and Miroslav Tadic's defence is over. We don't have any new evidence. And I can't believe that new documents regarding the Crisis Staff are now presented, now when Miroslav Tadic's Defence cannot present any evidence that could dispute the facts that have now been raised in the cross-examination. Earlier on I've already said the Prosecution, if they've had such a document in their possession since 1996 or even earlier should have disclosed such documents to us. If the Prosecution can now prove that the document is new, then I think our Defence should be given the chance to say something about this document, not necessarily to examine this witness but to prove the facts. As far as I know, all the members of the Executive Board were heard before this Tribunal, all the members of the Crisis Staff. My Defence, the Defence of Miroslav Tadic, is over, and now we are confronted with a document that could carry some weight, now at the end of the defence case. We really cannot tolerate, Your Honours, the fact that there have been several teams here in this courtroom and all of a sudden we have a new document. I am the second defence counsel for Mr. Tadic, and I saw all the documents before the trial, not before my case started but before the trial, and I really can't allow to have a new piece of evidence now. We are at the end of the Defence case and this is a relevant document and we can't allow for this document to be presented now, at such a late stage, unless the Prosecution can prove to us that it only arrived by that document -- day or the day before yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, his 92 bis statement was filed after the completion of Mr. Tadic's case, so if he has any complaint, it's with Mr. Pantelic, not with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. What the Trial Chamber wishes to elicit from the Prosecution is this: That is this document only going to deal with the appointment of in witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Strictly dealing with the appointment of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber is of the view that the document has probative value, and since it's restricted only to the appointment of this witness, and nothing else, the Prosecution is allowed to have it produced.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Can we have the number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The decision dated 25th of April, 1992, will be treated as Exhibit P181 for the English and P181 ter for the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
