utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, let us look at the top of the document, the top of the left -- top left portion. It says: "Serbian municipality of Bosanski Samac Crisis Staff." Does it not say that, sir?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And it's dated the 25th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And then it says, if you look at the next line: "Bearing in mind the need for vital institutions and organisations to continue their work, the Crisis Staff of the Serbian municipality of Bosanski Samac hereby adopts a decision." And it appoints you as Crisis Staff coordinator for the organisation of work and business transactions in Bosanka DD, Velepromet DD, and Posavka DD; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: This is what it says here. I see in document for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And it's signed on the bottom and stamped by the Crisis Staff, appointing you.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: I claim that I was never a member of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No. I'm not saying you were a member of the Crisis Staff, sir. I'm saying the document is signed on the bottom, and it has the seal of the Crisis Staff, this letter of appointment to you; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: I repeat: I've never seen this document before. This is the first time I see this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's not my question. It's signed on the bottom and it has the stamp of the Crisis Staff, of the Serbian municipality of Bosanski Samac; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: I can see a signature, but I don't know whose signature it is. And I also see the stamp of the Municipal Assembly of Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And this document appoints you to the position you described in paragraph 21, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: This is not the way I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Are you saying this isn't an appointment, sir, this document doesn't appoint you as the coordinator of Bosanka DD?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: I was appointed coordinator of Bosanka based on a document produced by the Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'd ask you to look at this document of appointment. Does it say Executive Board anywhere on the document?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Is the name of the Executive Board president, Mirko Jovanovic or, later, your cousin Milan Simic, on this document?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Not on this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Rather, at the bottom of the document, it says "municipal Crisis Staff," right above the signature.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff of the Assembly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And the decision, which is signed and stamped, of this document is an appointment of you as the coordinator, the Crisis Staff coordinator of the Bosanka company; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. In fairness to witness, my learned friend should make a proper quotation and reference of this document. It's not only Bosanka company, what it says in this document. It's three companies. So this witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's fair.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: -- clearly said in his statement, 92 bis statement, that he was appointed only for Bosanka company or coordinator by the Executive Board. It's paragraph 10. And if my learned friend would like to clarify this issue, he should follow the rules, rules of fairness. If in this document we have three companies, then we have to make a proper quotation. And in addition, this witness, on numerous occasions, just ten minutes ago, said that's the first time he saw this document. So I really don't know what is the purpose of this examination, but I leave it to my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, in his paragraph 10, if you want to look at his 92 bis statement, he refers to the merger of the three companies, and he's referred to it today as the Bosanka company and later it becomes the Samcanka company.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. He's speaking about his position of coordinator for company Bosanka by the Executive Board, which, after a year became known as another company. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Just be precise, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's just what my question was. He just said his position as coordinator for the Bosanka company and that's what I just said to him, to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Which is not a part of this document. That was the basis of my objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic. That is noted. Mr. Weiner, can you go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, it indicates that you were appointed the coordinator of these three companies, doesn't it, sir? It's a decision by the Crisis Staff appointing you as coordinator of these three companies, which later becomes the Samcanka, if I've pronounced it right, company.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: I was appointed coordinator of a state-owned company called Bosanka. When Samcanka was established, when that company was established, I became the coordinator of the company Samcanka, and that company was established --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The question here is: This document is a decision appointing you as Crisis Staff coordinator of Bosanka, Velepromet, and Posavanka, which later becomes, as you've testified, Samcanka. Doesn't it appoint you as Crisis Staff coordinator of those three companies, this document here?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: According to the decision of the Executive Board, I was appointed coordinator of the company called Bosanka.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, my question is: I want you to look at this document. This document here in front of you is a decision appointing you as the Crisis Staff coordinator of Bosanka, Velepromet, and Posavanka or Posavka, isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: This is what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on. Thank you. Sir, you mentioned in paragraph 21 of your statement that organised and individual looting was prevented in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: According to my own personal knowledge, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Are you aware that we've had several witnesses testify in this case concerning looting in this municipality and that testimony has not been contested? Are you aware of that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Objection. Your Honour, number 1, we have a clear ruling of this Honourable Trial Chamber with regard to the confrontment of a witness with the previous testimonies of witnesses. Number 2, if my learned friend can be more specific, saying on which occasion that was testimony, which witness, and when it was not contested by the Defence. Otherwise it's too general and it might be confusing for this witness. Maybe my learned friend could be more specific. I'm not objecting to the line of questioning. It's just --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'd be happy to. Thank you, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Are you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: There is no need for that, Mr. Pantelic. There is only one point I wanted to be clear with you. Are you saying that that evidence concerning looting is contested?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: We, on many occasions, contested so-called organised looting, which Prosecutor alleges against our clients, including our witnesses, we gave the evidence that particular events during the wartime, as looting by individuals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Because here, in paragraph 21, we have to separate. Because he says during the war organised and individual looting, which can cause confusion. The Defence was -- Mr. Pantelic is saying that the allegation on organised looting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: They haven't contested the fact that there was in fact -- that there was looting. They've contested that their clients were involved in it. And my question is strictly that we've had a lot of evidence in relation to acts of looting, extensive organised acts of looting occurring. On a few -- where the defendant Zaric makes a statement implicating his client, I will confront the witness with that. But strictly, all I'm saying is there's been extensive testimony here and I can give the Court the cites.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. There is this testimony, especially from the Prosecution witnesses, which is on record.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, my question to you, sir: Are you aware that several witnesses have testified about extensive looting in the municipality of Bosanski Samac, and that information was not contested by the defendants? Are you aware of that, sir?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: The fact that some witnesses came to testify to that effect, I don't know about it. But with regards to the organised looting, I also have no knowledge about it. I only know that there was the army. The army went from one place to the other. And I can tell you that there was an attempt to prevent individual theft and looting of some items and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Are you aware that your brother, the defendant Blagoje Simic, has testified of his knowledge of the theft of vehicles by Serbian volunteers and paramilitaries? Were you aware of that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: For counsel, it's at page 12.453 through 56.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were you aware that the defendant Blagoje Simic has testified about the constant problem of military looting of private and socially owned property, he testified about that at pages 12.327 through 331? Were you aware of that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, in order to be precise and fair to this witness, it's a double-barrelled question, whether he's aware the defendant said that or it occurred in the municipality of Samac? Let's be clear, because otherwise it's not so clear in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: My question is clear. I'm asking him if he's aware of the testimony.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Are you aware that the defendant Simo Zaric has given a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor on April 2nd, 1998 - it's Exhibit 141 ter - describing extensive and organised looting occurring in Odzak? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Are you aware that in that same interview with the Prosecutor's office, the defendant Zaric implicated your brother, the defendant Blagoje Simic, and Stevan Todorovic and the Crisis Staff in the looting of Odzak? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were you aware that Stevan Todorovic has admitted as part of his plea of guilt of persecution to the non-Serb -- persecution of the non-Serb population that he has admitted to the looting of non-Serb dwellings, businesses, personal property, and livestock? Were you aware of that, sir?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Finally, sir, were you aware that in a report signed by 13 officers of the command staff of the 2nd Posavina Brigade, it mentions that in Bosanski Samac there was looting of shops and private houses, with the assistance of the civilian and military authorities, and further notes that the looting was organised? Were you aware of that, sir?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, knowing that -- or now being aware of these complaints about looting occurring in Bosanski Samac, these complaints by witnesses, the defendant Zaric, the chief of police at the time, Stevan Todorovic, who has admitted his involvement in it, by the military command of the 2nd Posavina Brigade and by your brother, who describes looting of the volunteers and army, do you wish to change your statement in paragraph 21 that looting was prevented in the municipality of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: What I know is that there was probably some theft of private goods, but it was always prevented in the sense that we were always -- or it was always attempted to prevent an organised looting. That was prevented. What I know is when it comes to certain goods and items, those were under the control, and it's the reserves that had the control over it. And because I was the coordinator of the state-owned companies, and since I was in charge of the goods belonging to those companies, I did not get involved into this kind of theft of private goods.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, the question is: Recognising the statements of several individuals concerning looting in Bosanski Samac, including the police chief, who was responsible to stop looting, his admission that he was involved in looting, do you wish to change your statement that looting was prevented? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, if you look at the answer of this witness, he has explained his side of the story, so I don't see why you should insist.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You said that it was prevented, sir. The person who was responsible for preventing looting is the police chief. However, do you realise in Bosanski Samac the police chief has admitted to being involved in extensive looting? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: I've already stated that the looting and theft of goods was prevented. Now, to what extent it was prevented, I don't know. I've put this down in writing, saying that there had been some individual theft but that there was always an attempt to prevent it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, once again, the person responsible for preventing it has admitted to being involved in the looting, Stevan Todorovic. Are you aware of that, sir?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let's go to one more topic, sir. You mention you're the older brother to Blagoje Simic, the defendant in this case. And as his older brother, did you ever advise him concerning his decisions and actions and those of the Crisis Staff? Did you ever criticise to him at these family gatherings actions of the Crisis Staff or War Presidency? Did you ever advise him, as his older brother?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: As an older brother, I did talk to my brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And did you tell him, sir, that certain actions of the Crisis Staff were wrong, or at least demonstrated poor judgement? Did you tell him that, as his older brother?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, I won't allow this type of questioning. It isn't fair to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right, sir. Let's finish off with this. You worked with a Mr. Jusufovic; isn't that correct, Jusuf Jusufovic?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And are you aware that he was related to a Lirija or a Dr. Jusufovic, Lirija Jusufovic?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: I don't know which Dr. Jusufovic you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: A woman named Lirija. She worked at the medical centre. Were you aware -- let's take it this way. Did you attend a wedding between -- did you attend a wedding between Crni, the head of the paramilitaries, and Lirija Jusufovic, or Dr. Lirija Jusufovic?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Are you aware that your brother attended that wedding, the defendant Blagoje Simic, between Dr. Jusufovic and the head of the Serbian paramilitaries or volunteers, named Crni, or nicknamed Crni?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Are you aware that your brother, the defendant Blagoje Simic, served as Crni's best man, or kum, as you would say in your country, at this wedding, the wedding of the head of the paramilitaries and Dr. Lirija Jusufovic? Are you aware of that, sir?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Does that demonstrate to you poor judgement, where your brother has served as best man in the wedding of the head of the paramilitaries? Would you agree with me that it demonstrates poor judgement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, Mr. Weiner. I will not allow that question. It's not fair to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I just for a second approach my client --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: -- to get instructions, please. Thank you. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. You can go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It's absolutely new fact for me, this episode, so I just consulted my client and he said that he never was --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Objection to that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, no, no. You re-examine the witness, Mr. Pantelic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, did your brother ever tell you that he never was a best man at a wedding, or a kum? Did you ever talk about this?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: No. If I recall correctly, we never spoke about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Very well. With regards to this relationship that the Prosecutor attempted to establish, this family tie, let us clarify something for the transcript. The municipality of Samac was composed of approximately 30.000 inhabitants, according to the census of 1990.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes. We were 33.000 inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your family comes from a village called Kruskovo Polje, which is part of the municipality of Samac; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: How many inhabitants live at Kruskovo Polje, approximately?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Approximately 400 to 500 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: How would you describe the last name Simic? Is it a name that is -- is it a familiar name? Is it a name that comes often in that area, in Posavina?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Almost all local communes on the municipality have that name Simic, and lots of municipalities of Bosnia-Herzegovina as well, and you will find that name in lots of municipalities of Yugoslavia, that is, Serbia and Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: But we're talking about Simeon Simic now. Your father and the father of Simeon Simic, are they family? Are they brothers?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your grandfather and the grandfather of Simeon Simic, are they brothers?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your great-grandfather and the great-grandfather of Simeon Simic, are they brothers?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: No, but they were first cousins.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So your great-grandfather and the great-grandfather of Simeon Simic are some kind of relatives but they are not brothers?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: No, they're not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to clarify this for the transcript, because I wanted the Prosecutor to understand these things. Now let's talk about Milan Simic. Your father and the father of Milan Simic, are they brothers?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your grandfather and the grandfather of Milan Simic, are they brothers?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your great-grandfather and the great-grandfather of Milan Simic, are they brothers?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And finally, was Milan Simic married in 1992 with a cousin of Stevan Todorovic?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Were they -- in 1992, were they married officially? Do you know that? Do you have this knowledge?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: No, I do not have knowledge of the fact that they were officially married.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Pantelic. If I can just interject with one question for clarification. You've just asked the witness Mr. Simic about the ancestry, shall we say, of Mr. Milan Simic and we see now that the grandfathers and great-grandfathers weren't brothers. But I wonder whether Mr. Simic could tell us as to his knowledge as to whether there was a familial connection between Mr. Milan Simic and Dr. Blagoje Simic, and obviously also the witness himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I will do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This being said, could you please explain to Judge Williams what is the family connection? Because in Serbia we're all in a way cousins in some kind of way.

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: It's an old family. They came to that area of Bosnia and Herzegovina 150 years ago. And since that family grew and all the Simic come from that family, so everything I said so far is true in the sense that we all have the same last name, but those families are connected, but it's a family connection that is quite distant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: So you can't with any, therefore, accuracy say that Mr. Milan Simic and Dr. Blagoje Simic were cousins or anything of that description? You simply say there's some connection, traceable way back, but you can't exactly define it; is that the case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to our own terminology in Bosnia and Herzegovina, we call each other cousins. That is to say, everybody who within one same family bears the same last name is a cousin. Now, when you go back four to five generations, then we can see that their great-grandfathers were not brothers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you for your attention to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: To conclude: The Simic are something like the Smith family in Great Britain, for instance?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I object.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I withdraw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, can you get on with your examination. We have other witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only one question pertaining to this line of questioning that the Prosecutor opened with regards to the candidates. Simeon Simic was the first on the list of the party called SSO. It's the abbreviation for the Association of Youth, Socialist Youth; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Later on, this association became the Liberal Party, headed by a Muslim called Rasim Kadic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Do you know if Milan Simic was to get married at the very beginning of 1993, but he did not get married because he had an accident? Do you know of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I object. It's outside the scope of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Simic: You're not a lawyer and you do not have any particular knowledge about the constitution?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: When you were answering a question of the Prosecutor with regards to the Municipal Assembly being the highest authority or highest organ, did you think of it in the legislative way?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the legislative way, and in a more narrow meaning it is the Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And my very last question. If you know, please tell us and tell the Trial Chamber: What was the procedure when the decisions were adopted within the Executive Board? Were they passing some kind of drafts and then the drafts were adopted after being proposed to the Crisis Staff? If you know, please tell us?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'd object again. This is outside the scope of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It is within the scope, Your Honour, with all due respect, because we have discussed Exhibit P181. My learned friend raised the issue, relations between Executive Board and Crisis Staff. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, I will allow it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will reiterate my question. So according to your knowledge and according to your experience, can you tell us if the organs of the Executive Board prepare a draft to propose it to the Executive Board and was that the case during the wartime presidency?

utterances.speaker: CEDOMIR SIMIC
utterances.text: I told you what I knew about the Executive Board and what my experience was. I was in charge of the goods and distributing the goods and the needs of the municipalities, but I was not involved in whatever else the Executive Board had to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I've finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Simic. I just have one question. You mentioned, on page 47, lines 7 and 8, in response to a question by the Prosecutor, that -- well, I'll quote. You said: "I was appointed coordinator of Bosanka, based on a document produced by the Executive Board." And I'm just wondering: Was this document put into your hands? Do you still retain it in your personal records? Because clearly we haven't got such a document in front of us. We only have the document that was produced by the Prosecutor, Exhibit P181. So I'm just interested in learning a little bit more about the document that you say was produced by the Executive Board appointing you coordinator of Bosanka, if you have some more information on that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's been 11 years since, and I have forgotten a lot of things. However, all the documents in my possession, in my private archive, are related to the Executive Board. And I think I should have the document we're talking about somewhere, the document on my appointment by the president of the Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Simic. We are finished with your evidence. You may leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can the witness make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. Will you please state your name for the record, please.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: Lazar Mirkic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mirkic, good afternoon. I have a number of questions for you related to the Rule 92 bis procedure and statement you gave. One section of a paragraph must be gone through here in live testimony, and it is in this context that I will ask you a number of questions. As we speak the same language, please, after my question make a short pause, for the benefit of the interpreters interpreting your testimony into the official languages of the Tribunal and to keep the transcript accurate, please. Mr. Mirkic, your personal information, family information, information concerning your profession, are included in paragraph 1 of your statement, but I must ask you the following question: In 1992, were you a member of any party?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In 1992, among businessmen in the circles in which you moved, because you were a manager, did you hold any official positions or posts? What were your positions in those circles? What were your ratings? How did your business partners work with you? Did you have any problems or was it smooth for all those involved?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: In the system that we had of the economy, I enjoyed some degree of notable success, and I was rated as a very successful manager. I was held in high esteem by both the people I worked with and with common citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did you also work with international companies or foreign companies?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, a great deal. Mostly with Italy, Greece, what used to be Czechoslovakia, Hungary, and we exported lamb meat to Kuwait.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, Mr. Mirkic, are you now a member of any political party?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: Yell.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Which one?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: The Serbian Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Since when?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: Since June 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In 1992, you were the manager of Agroposavina based in Donji Zabar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, and I had been in 1995 all the way to late 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Now you're the owner and manager of a private company called Agreks?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: I am the owner of the Agreks company. I am not the manager, however.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Would you just bear with me for a second to check the transcript. Just a correction for the transcript. On page 64, line 14, the witness said in 1992 he was a manager of Agroposavina company based in Donji Zabar. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your company, Agreks, is in international trade, domestic trade, that sort of thing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, can we go to what is relevant for this case, please, and these are the matters concerning the relationship between the Executive Board, the Crisis Staff, the War Presidency --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: And also the relationship with the army institutions. That is what is relevant in this case and that is what the focus of this witness should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'll do that. Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tell me, please: Where were you when war conflict broke out on the 16th and 17th of April, 1992, you personally? What was your location?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: I was in Donji Zabar and in Pelagicevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Where was your family?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: In Pelagicevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Where did you reside with your family prior to that period of time?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: In Orasje.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: When did you leave Orasje?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: I believe it was the 26th of September, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What was the reason for you and your family to leave Orasje?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: Just across the River Sava there was war in Croatia, and I think it was on that day that the bridge over the River Sava was destroyed, linking Bosnia and Herzegovina to Croatia. This was an unpleasant thing for the citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you, Mr. Mirkic. What was the reason that you and your family left for Pelagicevo? Just briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: Safety, personal safety.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Had you received any threats in Orasje, you and your family?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: There had been telephone calls to our home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, I think the Trial Chamber has given you instructions as to what the focus should be of this witness. Otherwise, we shall declare the witness finished, as far as you're concerned, and then we'll allow cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Because you're going completely outside what the witness is to discuss.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Because I just want to go to the moment of his appointment as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, that's not necessary. Just deal with the matters that I directed you to.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it's an agreed fact from your statement and from the documents we have before us now that you were appointed secretary for the economy, a member of the Executive Board of the Serbian municipality of Samac and Pelagicevo that was on a meeting held on the 28th of March, 1992. My question is the following: Since when have you worked in the economy of the Pelagicevo and Samac municipalities, in terms of dates?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: After the conflict broke out in the night between the 16th and the 17th of April, I remained in the Pelagicevo and Zabar area. I made certain efforts for the security in our company to function properly, the company of which I was manager. Because a large number of employees had been mobilised, drafted into the army, and other employees, those of Muslim and Croatian ethnicity, remained at their homes. So we agreed that they would work in that area where we had farms, milking cows, and an engine shed, we believed that the conflict would soon come to an end and that we could keep on doing our daily business as usual.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What was the basis for your appointment as secretary for the economy? More specifically, had there been a decision on a work assignment or had there been a different document appointing you to that position?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: All men of military age and all able-bodied men had their war assignments and there had to be military decision assigning them to a certain post, a post assigned to them by their war assignments or by another document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Specifically, what was yours? Did you receive a decision to that effect?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: No. I received no decision at that time, and I think at that time there were many people like me who received no decisions in writing. From the army, we did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In the area that you were covering, the Pelagicevo municipality, which was part of the newly created Samac and Pelagicevo municipalities, can you please explain to the Trial Chamber, as secretary for the economy of this newly created municipality, what were your tasks? Did you have anyone assisting you, as secretary, and you personally, as of the 18th of April, what were your tasks and duties?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: My assistants were Milan Simic, for the industry. There was an oral agreement for him to stay in the town of Samac and to cover our activities there. Aleksa Stakic from Pelagicevo was my assistant for agriculture, and I usually coordinated their work, the work of those two, in those moments when we could actually communicate.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Can you please describe for the Trial Chamber your activities following the 18th of April in the area where you worked?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: It is known that the conflict broke out just before the spring sowing, and this had to be secured throughout the area for the season. We had to secure the materials, the raw materials. We were running out of those. We had to secure manpower to carry out this task. We had to secure the equipment and the machines necessary for that. We had to secure the sowing in those families where most members of the family had been mobilised, leaving at home people who were not as physically able to do such hard work. We also got the civilian protection involved on that, which included people who were not military conscripts or people liable for military service. We often provided the mechanical equipment so that the sowing could be done in spring season.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In the first days of war, what steps did you take as secretary for the economy to secure normal supplies for the civilian population, in your own area of work? Which measures did you take, if any?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: One of the most important measures was to protect from -- to preserve from destruction our own reserves, what we had in stock, what we had across companies, co-ops and other buildings and facilities. This was absolutely imperative, for us to preserve this so that we could do the sowing. And on the other hand, it enabled us to supply all the necessary goods, those necessary for survival of the population under those difficult circumstances. When there was shelling on a daily basis, people were getting killed every day, sometimes even several people a day, many things had to be preserved. We had to go so far as to start the production of coffins for dead bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Very well. What I want to know is about the sector of work or area of work that you covered, that you were in charge of. Did you secure supplies for the whole civilian population or only for some ethnic groups, as opposed to others? Please tell the Trial Chamber first of all about the different ethnic groups living in the area, and what was your relationship to the civilian population as a whole? Was there any discrimination on the basis of ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: There was no form of ethnic discrimination; quite the contrary. I think it was the other ethnic groups that were quite well served, I should say, and profusely supplied with staple foods and consumer goods, because they were mostly based in the town of Samac itself. Serbs lived in the surrounding villages also. And then it was easier to get food items for personal hygiene, that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In Pelagicevo, which was your area in terms of the economy, were there any Muslims and Croats there?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: No. That was a Serb village.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I mean the general area. I don't mean the village itself only. I'm referring to Obudovac and the surroundings.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: All of those were Serb villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In your company, in Agroposavina, did you have employees of other nationalities?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did they continue to work after the conflict broke out?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: Most of the Croats and Muslims working there remained in the company, in a unit, a work unit that was based in Orasje, and this unit was part of our company. That was an agreement that they had with me, that they would remain there and carry out certain tasks, because we had a farm there where we milked cows. There was an engine shed there where we kept machines and a place where we kept fodder.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Can you please clarify this: Orasje, is it in the territory of Republika Srpska or is it in the Croatian Muslim Federation?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: It's in the territories of the Muslim Croatian Federation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In 1992, was this Croatian-controlled territory?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What was your activity with the Executive Board about? Please explain this to the Trial Chamber. How often did you go to meetings? What was discussed at those meetings? Which steps did you take as a member of the Executive Board in charge of the economy?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: I didn't go to Samac very often. I didn't go to the Executive Board in Samac very often, because that area was covered by another man who was in charge of organising the economy there. I went when I was especially called by the president of the Executive Board, Mirko Jovanovic, personally, initially, and later it was Mr. Simic. Those were mostly brief meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: When you say "Mr. Simic," for the sake of precision, which seem are you referring to? Because there are quite many of them.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: Milan Simic. And the president of the Executive Board was very considerate in terms of my obligations back in the company, because we had bioproduction, and there were frequent power failures. We had problems with power failures. We had 1.052 head of cattle, and the lack of fodder had to be made good. It took superhuman efforts to deliver all our products to the market in this period of hyperinflation. It required superhuman efforts to preserve all of this and to preserve the real value of what we had. This was absolutely imperative for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mirkic, tell me, please: During your work with the Executive Board, what was the hierarchy of the Executive Board like? Which regulations did they apply? Can you please explain the link between the Executive Board and the government of Republika Srpska at that time, as far as you're familiar with it and as far as the economy is concerned.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: It was a vertical connection up to the relevant ministries, the government's ministries, the government of Republika Srpska, and vice versa. There was frequent coordination. Mostly it went through the president or chairman of the Executive Board, who then provided us with instructions on what we should do and how we should work.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mirkic, as far as the link to the army was concerned, what were the regulations there, and what were the obligations of different people in the economy or companies, and the Executive Board itself to the army? MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, this evidence is rapidly becoming incomprehensible in my submission. Page 71, line 13, there are three separate questions in the question. In the answer, there's reference to a vertical connection up to relevant ministries, frequent coordination. Vertical connection between what and whom? What ministries? "Frequent coordination," what does that mean? "Mostly it went through the president or chairman of the Executive Board." That doesn't mean anything. The next question that you have following that is a link to the army, what the regulations, what the obligations of different people in the economy or companies, and the Executive Board itself to the army. If the witness gives an answer to that question, you won't know what he's answering, because it's just so utterly imprecise. Now, you want this evidence to have meaning, you've got to have a little more precision than all of that, in my submission, otherwise it's just -- you don't know what he's talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Maybe it's a matter of translation. But I will try to clarify that as much as possible, just for the information of my learned friend, he can find the very precise answer that the ministries in question, that's page 71, line 18 and 19, the ministries in question actually was the part of the government of Republika Srpska. So it's very clear about which ministries we are speaking. But I will clarify again that with the witness. No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Mr. Mirkic, tell me, please: You spoke about the vertical line connecting the Executive Board with the relevant ministries. On the basis of which provisions or regulations, tell us, please, if you know, did that link connecting them exist? More specifically, were those informal connections or did organs of the ministries adopt any enactments or anything? Tell us, if you know.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: I could tell you about the ministry of the economy -- of agriculture. Mr. Mlivoje Nadedin was the minister in the joint government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and he was later minister with the republican government of Republika Srpska. We kept in touch with him and we consulted him on a number of issues. We requested his assistance in certain wartime situations. I was not in charge of any other links or connections, nor was I in charge of establishing contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Very well. Certain ministries adopt certain enactments; is that so? You are a person working in the field of the economy, a well-known person, so what would these enactments be, those passed by the relevant ministries?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: Provisions, decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In 1992, you at the Executive Board, did you carry out or implement those provisions or decisions by the government in the field of economy?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Further, we're talking about the army. This is wartime we're talking about. So what is the role of the economy in wartime, wartime economy? Can you please explain this to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: It was a simple question we businessmen were facing: How will the economy survive the war? And we did the best we could. We worked to the best of our ability. It was preservation work. We wanted to preserve the companies, the employees, our personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And what were the obligations of the economy towards the Ministry of Defence? What were the obligations of the economy and the companies towards the army of Republika Srpska? Can you please explain that? And what were these obligations really based on?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: I don't think I can provide a specific answer to this one, save for what I know. I know that the company sold some items to the army, beef, and we charged them for this. This didn't come free of charge. It's only to be expected in such a time that logistical supplies were set up, that the army was assisted and that they were given some items necessary for their proper functioning. All the more so because the army was made up of volunteers, of locals who had been mobilised. All of them were neighbours, friends, brothers, relatives, people we knew. It would have been impossible for us not to secure sufficient food for them. We did whatever we could.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: This obligation, did it comprise providing the military with accommodation, with food, with supplies, supplying their uniforms even?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: Mostly it was about food and some uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What were your obligations, you as a businessman and as secretary for the economy, towards the republican commodity reserves in wartime?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: Later on I heard that a prescription had been published for all goods found, collected, to become the property of the republican commodity reserves. I myself did not work on these tasks, and I can't really tell you anything very specific about this question of yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Appropriate time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, we'll take our break.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mirkic, before the break we were talking about the authorities and the relationship between the Executive Board and other bodies, primarily ministries. Please tell me: Do you have any personal knowledge of the way decisions were drafted in the Executive Board when it came to different areas that had to be covered by that body? Did you have expert services, technical services? What were the discussions like? Could you please explain that to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: We didn't have very big technical services. A lot of things were done in a haste, day in, day out, according to the situation. So we were reactive rather than proactive. There were very few things that we could really plan for a longer-term period.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge about the fact that some decisions were drafted by the secretariat and then proposed to the Executive Board for adoption?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Some certainly were. Mostly those that concerned various sectors.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You were a member of the Executive Board, that is, the secretary for economics, up to the end of July 1992; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Who replaced you in the Executive Board of Samac municipality as the secretary for economy, if you know?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do know. It was Mr. Slobodan Simic [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat his last name?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: It is not Simic, but Sijencic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: How often during the period while you held that post and later on, in 1992, 1993, did you have contacts, personal contacts, with Dr. Blagoje Simic? Can you remember?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: I had very few contacts with him, save for one occasion when Dr. Blagoje Simic visited the area where I resided and worked. He wanted to gather information on the functioning of the civilian protection. And then the two of us together visited the office in my native village, in Covic Polje, which was under a big threat because it was on the line of fire. It was a very poor village. And we wanted to know how people managed, how they manage to survive, what they needed, what they required. And then Dr. Simic asked the civilian protection to be of assistance to the poorest segment of the population, primarily those who had lost members of their family to the war and returnees. Later on we would only come across each other on one or two occasions, but we didn't have any close contacts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What was the situation with refugees in your area where you resided? If there were refugees, how did you deal with their problems?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: Refugees would come to my company. They would come from Orasje and from Serbian villages in Odzak municipality, and maybe from some other places from one side or another. We had a furniture store, and women and children were accommodated there. They would be given tea or milk for children, and other necessities, and then they would find their own way to go elsewhere, where they would find more permanent accommodation and wait for the war to be over, for the conflict to come to an end.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mirkic, in those contacts with Dr. Blagoje Simic, what were his comments and what was his attitude towards other ethnic groups, non-Serbs? Did he show any sort of intolerance? What were his comments?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: I never heard anything that would -- that could be characterised as discrimination of other ethnic groups. I really never hear Blagoje advocating any sort of discrimination.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And finally, tell me, if you know: What was the relationship between the civilian authorities and the army and the police? In other words, was the civilian government in the position to issue orders to the military and to the police?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: We had absolutely no contacts with the structures in the police and in the army. There is no way we could influence the command structures or any events involving the military or the police. The situation was the following: The Executive Board did have no authority whatsoever to control the work of the police. The police was linked to the minister of the interior and his associates, and the ministry as a whole. So I claim with full responsibility that we did not have any control over the work of the police or any influence on their work.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And as regards the army of Republika Srpska, the army structures, what was the situation there?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: My previous answer could also apply to this question. It would be much the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Employees working in the companies in the region where you were in charge of the coordination of the economy, did the employees receive salaries in 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Were there contributions paid as well, the pension contribution and the medical insurance?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were paid, but when we couldn't do it in due time, then we would pay the back contributions. That was the principle, and I believe that one could check that in the files, in the municipal files, and one could verify whether all these contributions were paid. But generally speaking, there was the principle that we honoured, and that was to pay the contributions, because for that matter, our activities were funded from the funds.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Was there a selective approach or did that apply to all the three ethnic backgrounds?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: There was no selective approach. All the employees enjoy the same rights and had the same obligations towards their workplace. So we never talked about or received any instruction to the effect of somebody being privileged in any sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And finally, during 1992 and 1993, was the economic situation normal or was there inflation? If there was, how was the issue of salaries dealt with?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: I believe that it will be inconceivable for all those who come from other economic systems, but let me tell you that there was such a high rate of inflation that when you were clinching a certain business deal, we would also negotiate the price and the terms of payments in hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Why in hours?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: Because the new rate of exchange was established every half an hour. So that within the matter of hours, certain goods would lose 50 per cent of their value.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So how did you deal with the issue of salaries? Did you pay them in kind or did you resort to any other means?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, we would give them staple foods, flour, salt, washing powder. And it is correct to say that employees preferred to be paid in kind than to be paid in cash, because money was losing its value very fast, and everybody needed food, and food kept its constant value.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Any other counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: We have no questions for this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pisarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, we don't have any questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Mr. Mirkic, my name is Mr. Di Fazio. I have a few questions for you on behalf of the Prosecution. I want to ask you about your appointment to the Executive Board, and you described that process in paragraph 8 of your statement, and you say that in late March or early April, Mirko Jovanovic called you --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I do apologise to my learned friend. Could we have a copy in B/C/S language, for the sake -- MR. DI FAZIO: I didn't realize. Yes. Could the witness be given his statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll manage. Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You say that, in your statement, paragraph 8, that Mirko Jovanovic called you and asked you to join the Executive Board. Up until that point in time, had you had any idea that this request was going to be made, or did it come as a surprise to you?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: It came as an utter surprise.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: At the time, where were you residing?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: I was residing with my in-laws in Pelagicevo. That is where my child went to school.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And you were busily engaged in carrying on your occupation as the manager of a company?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You have no formal economic qualifications, do you?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: I'm an engineer. I have a degree in agriculture.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Right. Fine. That's what I understood. So you've got qualifications as an engineer and you have a degree in agriculture, and you have experience as a businessman running a company, but you have no formal economic qualifications, do you, the study of economics?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: That is correct. I managed the company since 1985, in a very successful way.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I don't doubt that, but your experience in business is confined to running a company. Correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Furthermore, you didn't have any particular knowledge of the situation in Bosanski Samac, in the town and in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you point out these matters to Mr. Jovanovic when he contacted you and made the request that you join the Executive Board?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did tell him that. But a compromise was reached, according to which Mr. Milan Simic would be my assistant, who would be in charge of industry. He has a degree in economics and he also had experience to carry out those tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Was that agreement reached on the occasion that you were first contacted or was that sorted out later, after your acceptance of the post?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: I believe that later on, at the session of the Assembly which was held on the 28th of March, I was proposed to be a member of the cabinet, and then since my positions were contrary to his, he reassured me. He told me everything would be okay, that everything would be covered very well, that he would give me qualified assistants, and that my role was to use my authority to satisfy the population that things would be run smoothly, because people placed a lot of trust in me and my work.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: So the sequence was that Mirko Jovanovic contacted you first, asking you to join the Executive Board; subsequently, in late March, your appointment was formally adopted by the Municipal Assembly, the Serbian Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: No. It was a bit different. The Assembly session was first. It took place on the 28th of March. Later on I was informed by Mirko what had taken place at the session. He told me that I had been proposed as a member of his cabinet. And then the rest of my previous answer applies to this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. That's what I thought from reading your statement. So you were proposed and appointed as director of municipal public revenues administration -- sorry. My apologies. My apologies. You were proposed and appointed as secretary of the municipal secretariat for the economy, without even having been spoken to about that possibility, about that position?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You didn't attend the session held on the 28th of March, 1992, where that appointment was made?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Were you surprised? Were you surprised when you learnt of your appointment?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, I was. I was not very familiar with Samac and its economy. The only part I was familiar with was agriculture. But I was reassured by him. He said that agriculture is the core business activity of our municipalities. He said I had the necessary experience to perform these duties correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: In addition to not being consulted about the position, in addition to that, you were being asked to join a body that was being set up parallel to the already existing and democratically elected organs in Bosanski Samac, weren't you? Or to put it another way, you knew that there was already an existing Municipal Assembly democratically collected in 1990, with all its attendant bodies, its own Executive Board, and so on. What you were being asked to do was to join a parallel, if you want to describe it that way, Executive Board. Did they ask you if you approved of that?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: That particular session of the Serbian Assembly of Samac municipality which was held in March 1992 carried the legitimacy of the previous elections, because it was composed of the elected deputies who were elected in 1990. They were all Serbs and representatives of all parties. Following the same line of logic, the Executive Board also was given the same legitimacy of that Assembly. The fact that it was not operational at the moment when it was appointed doesn't make a difference. It was said that both the Executive Board and the Assembly would start working at the moment when Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina, that is, the Serbian community, would be put into an unequal position with regard to other ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Is that what was going through your mind at the time, that you decided to accept the position? Is that your reasoning? Was that your reasoning? Did you take that into account, what you've just told us?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: I have taken that into account. I had taken it into account. And I believed and I was convinced that another solution would be found and that we would never have to behave like an independent Serbian organ. I was sure that we would find a solution, especially because the international community got involved in the process of talks which took place at the level of Bosnia and Herzegovina, including all the constitutive people which made or comprised the peoples of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I believed in this. But unfortunately, after a few attempts, it did not work out and we found ourselves precisely where we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: It goes without saying, of course, that in April -- sorry - in March and April of 1992, people in -- there were three ethnic groups living in Bosanski Samac, weren't there: The Croats, the Muslims, and the Serbs? Correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: This new body, the Executive Board, would be taking -- for it to make any sense, would be taking decisions, affecting the lives of all the people living in Bosanski Samac and the municipality of Bosanski Samac. Correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You would be participating in those decisions and those processes if you accepted your appointment. Correct?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, with the exception that my duties were strictly confined to my own sector, and I believe that I was competent to behave adequately in given situations [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. The body in which you were a member was going to start taking decisions which would affect the lives of Croats and Muslims, would it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I do apologise. Just in order to -- for the sake of clarity of the transcript. In page 84, line 22, after the full stop, actually, the other part which was not recorded of the statement of this witness, given the situation and in order to satisfy all people, all nations, and all community in Samac. MR. DI FAZIO: I'm sure that Mr. Pantelic heard correctly, and I accept that, and perhaps we can proceed now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: So the new Executive Board was going to take -- of which you were a member, had accepted membership, was going to take decisions, take actions that were going to affect the lives of all three -- members of all three ethnic groups. That's so, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And you accept, don't you, that the municipal -- the new Serbian Municipal Assembly, and later its incarnation as the Crisis Staff and the War Presidency, represented only Serbian people, don't you?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: I believe not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You knew, didn't you, that the Municipal Assembly only had appointed as deputies members of Serb -- members of the SDS and other parties who were of Serbian ethnicity? You knew that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: I did not know who was making the Assembly, who was part of it. I believe that it was an open possibility for all ethnicities to participate, but I believe and I suppose the majority was Serb, of Serb nationality. Now, I don't know who was -- who were the members of the Assembly. I do not know the exact ethnic structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You knew that the formal title of this new governmental body that was being announced in March and April of 1992 was the Municipal Assembly of the Serbian people of Bosanski Samac and Pelagicevo Under Formation; you knew that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: No, I did not know that. At the time, I did not know this. I saw it, however, later on, in some headlines.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Before or after your acceptance of your position in the Executive Board did you find out?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: After the acceptance, when the executive committee began its work. It may have been towards the middle of the month of May or perhaps end of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And you knew in March and April of 1992 that the Assembly of the Serbian people of Bosanski Samac and Pelagicevo was to consist of deputies of the Serbian Democratic Party of Bosanski Samac, Gradacac, Orasje, and Odzak; you knew that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: I think that this is not how it was specifically said. I believe that it was deputies of all ethnic groups and others who wished to be part of the Assembly. And I found that out later on because I did not take part in the works.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Before you -- if that be so, did you ever question the need of this particular Serbian municipality was, given the existence of an already democratically elected Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: It is a known fact that there was a polarisation on the basis of ethnicities, and this took place much earlier in Bosnia-Herzegovina and in other municipalities, as well as other areas. I believe that the Serbs were always behind other ethnic groups which lived in Bosnia and Herzegovina [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: That was your belief in 1992, and it's your belief now?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: In 1992, I did not have any precise knowledge of this, and later on I found out and I was able to read in the media, and I saw that the Croats also had their organisation, Croatian and Bosnian Posavina. They had their organs in their areas, in their localities. They had organised themselves in a similar fashion. They had their own municipal organs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. I do apologise to my learned friend. It's page 87, line 1. This witness said exactly the following: After the word "Herzegovina," he said in the sense of organisation." Because otherwise if we are reading this sentence, it might be somehow doubtful. MR. DI FAZIO: I accept what Mr. Pantelic says. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You've given evidence that you joined the SDS in 1996.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: By that time, 1996, you had had a good opportunity to observe its policies in action, to understand its policies, and you had no trouble or difficulty in joining the party, given that background knowledge, did you?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: What do you think of exactly? Could you please be more precise? I'm not sure if I understood your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Fair enough. I think my question was somewhat imprecise. I'll approach it another way. By 1996, you had seen the SDS at work for a period of at least six years. That is so, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You had seen it at work at both a national level and on a municipal level, and in particular in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: Yes, aside from one period of time when the work of all the parties was frozen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. And having seen its policies being carried into operation, you were pleased with those policies, considered them proper and just policies, and so you joined the party?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: I was not in charge of that. I was not governed by that, rather. And I believe that through the Dayton Accord through which the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina ended, I had the impression that the Dayton Accord proved that policy, but I did not get involved into the analysis of its work. I was governed by reputation of that party and the Serbian people had voted in majority for that party, and I thought that people for sure could not make a mistake. And maybe I was governed by that fact mainly. In terms of going more in depth with regards to the analysis of politics, I didn't do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. But let's get back to your appointment. In March of 1992, you had no formal economic qualifications, you didn't know what the political and economic situation was in Bosanski Samac, you had made no moves to join any of the organs or institutions of this new Serbian municipality. In those circumstances, the real reason that Jovanovic contacted you and asked you to accept a position in the Executive Board was that you sympathised with the policies of the SDS, you sympathised with the process that you could see unfolding in front of your eyes in March and April of 1992; that is so, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: I believe that I already answered that question, but I will try to be a little bit more clear. Mr. Jovanovic proposed my name as an expert for our circumstances, and I believe that I was an expert for the economy, especially when it comes to agriculture. With regards to politics, I was not very much involved in politics. I was an apolitical person. I was not even following whatever was going on in the world of politics. I wasn't following the events which took place in the city in which I lived. I was extremely busy in my company. And I really did not have time to get involved in other activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Why didn't you just refuse?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: For the simple reason that it was not asked of me to join immediately and to start working immediately, because I believed that it was only a temporary situation and that it would never be necessary to function, and to refuse it would have meant that I did not want to cooperate with the people, with my friends with whom I had been cooperating up until then. We were always good friends. So this is what I thought. And my answer to your question is simply that I never thought that I ever had to really do that work.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: What did you think you had to do?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: I thought that I was only going to do my own job. I believed in peace. I believed that in Bosnia there was going to be no war.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. The Executive Board of which you became a member was in fact a functioning, operational body in April, May, June, July, and throughout the remainder of the year, wasn't it? When I say that, I mean it carried out -- it held meetings, members participated in deliberations and discussions, and so on.

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: There were no meetings up until, I believe, the 18th of April. Afterwards, I heard that there had been one meeting, not only of the Executive Board but also of other structures, people who were worried with regards to the agricultural situation in the agricultural combine in Samac, and I suppose that these people were also in an extraordinary situation and they were trying to find a solution as to how to do something intelligent and how to resolve the problem, and I think that this is what they discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All I'm driving at is, it's a very simple thing: This Executive Board was a functioning organ in April, May, June, July, and throughout the remainder of that year, 1992. From time to time it held meetings. You may not have been there, but from time to time it held meetings, it took decisions, discussed policy. That's so, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: LAZAR MIRKIC
utterances.text: Policies were not discussed, but everything else was discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
